pr_title: Add support for UPSERT (INSERT .. ON CONFLICT DO ..) syntax
pr_body:
This PR fixes #61 

## Syntax

The syntax is the same as PostgreSQLs implementation:
```sql
INSERT INTO <table_name> ... ON CONFLICT <optional_columns_list> <optional_where_clause> DO NOTHING | DO UPDATE SET column_name = <optional 'excluded.' qualifier> column_name, ... <optional_where_clause>;
```
As a simple example of DO UPDATE:
```sql
insert into tbl VALUES (3,5,1) ON CONFLICT (i) WHERE k < 5 DO UPDATE SET k = 1;
```

## Overview

When performing the insert, we check for conflicts with UNIQUE/PRIMARY KEY constraints.
When a conflict arises, we check whether we should add this to the batch of ON CONFLICT tuples, or throw like normal.

To determine if we should add it to the batch, we look at:
The list columns, if it's empty we always move on to the second step, otherwise it needs to exactly match the columns of the constraint.
Next we check the first WHERE clause, only when that condition is met (or is left out) do we add it to the batch.
~~Any conflict that arises that does not meet *both* of those conditions causes an error to be thrown like normal.~~
When a non conflict_target conflict arises from an insert tuple that also caused a conflict in an index that **is** part of the conflict_target, the error is ignored.

DO NOTHING causes nothing to happen for those conflicts.
DO UPDATE SET expressions will alter the current record that was found to conflict with the to-be-inserted values.

Within the WHERE clauses and the SET expressions you can refer to both the tuple that already exists within the table: `column_name` 
And the tuple that you attempted to insert:
`excluded.column_name`

In the case of DO UPDATE, after the SET expressions you can define an additional WHERE clause, this is evaluated per tuple that was queued for an UPDATE.
Failing this condition does not cause the query to fail, instead it just turns the UPDATE into a `DO NOTHING` for that particular tuple.

## Known limitations:
- Only implicit Indexes (created by UNIQUE / PRIMARY key table constraints) are checked for the ON CONFLICT clause, other Indexes are only checked during transaction commit.
- ON CONFLICT ON CONSTRAINT is not supported yet, the only supported way to provide a `conflict_target` is by passing a list of column names.
- Only columns that are not indexed on can be assigned to in a DO UPDATE, no altering of columns that have unique/primary key constraints are supported by this functionality.
- `excluded.` qualified columns can not be part of a RETURNING clause.
- Batch insertion is not supported in combination with ON CONFLICT.

## Implementation differences:
- DO UPDATE is supported even when no `conflict_target` is provided, if and only if there is only one Index on the table.
pr_comments:
Just stumbled upon another (in my opinion) weird behavior of postgres
```sql
postgres=# insert into tbl(a,b) select 1,i from generate_series(1,50) as nums(i) on conflict (a) do update set b = excluded.b;
ERROR:  ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command cannot affect row a second time
HINT:  Ensure that no rows proposed for insertion within the same command have duplicate constrained values.
```

SQLite does accept the query:
```sqlite> insert into tbl(a,b) select 1, value from generate_series(1,50) where true on conflict (a) do update set b = excluded.b;
sqlite> select * from tbl;
1|50
```
As you can see it sets the value of b to the value of the last inserted tuple

In my implementation this is kind of undefined behavior currently, I was expecting postgres to just update to the last inserted tuple
Though if we keep in mind these are "sets" then there is no order, so "last inserted tuple" is also not well defined

To clarify a little further:
In my implementation, only one row of a chunk can affect an existing tuple:

```sql
statement ok
INSERT INTO integers(i) SELECT i from range(5000) tbl(i);

# Every insert tuple conflicts with the same existing tuple (the first one)
statement ok
insert into integers(i,j) select 0,i from range(5000) tbl(i) on conflict do update set j = excluded.j;

# Only the first value of the chunk got to update the value
# 0 is the first index of the first chunk
# 2048 is the first index of the second chunk
# 4096 is the first index of the last chunk
query I
select j from integers limit 1;
----
4096
```

This becomes undefined when we enable parallel insertion
So maybe you were right and I should stop INSERT from being parallel if it has an ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE clause
The DO NOTHING case could still be parallel though
Could you merge this with master again?

issue_context.title: Support for UPSERT statements
issue_context.body:
This is supported by both SQLite and PostgreSQL, so we probably should too

https://www.sqlite.org/lang_UPSERT.html
comments: I would argue that this is not critical for the first release
I am not able to find upsert in documentation is this release?

In case that gets tackled, I just want to add a kind request here: PostgreSQLimplements `UPSERT` with the `INSERT ON CONFLICT` statement. I've found this quite problematic when used in cases where generic code should be written against the database, since the statement must repeat all non-conflicting types for the `UPDATE` in the `ON CONFLICT` case.

I would significantly prefer a true `UPSERT` functionality, so anything that allows to write "insert this new data into a row if a corresponding row does not exist, or overwrite the corresponding row if one exists" as easily as possible.
Is there another open source database that implements this feature in a way that you particularly like? It always helps to have a good example! Thanks!

> Is there another open source database that implements this feature in a way that you particularly like? It always helps to have a good example! Thanks!

Admittedly, no, from the implementations that I've checked (PostgreSQL, SQLite and MySQL) the `UPSERT` is in my eyes always rather too "verbose". I can see some benefit in having the option of doing something different in the `ON CONFLICT` clause. But I'm always surprised that its *mandatory* to specify all non-conflicting entries again in the `ON CONFLICT` clause.

Considering from [here](https://www.techbeamers.com/mysql-upsert/) the following `ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` example:
```sql
INSERT INTO BLOGPOSTs (postId, postTitle, postPublished)
VALUES (5, 'Python Tutorial', '2019-08-04')
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE postId = 5, postTitle = 'Python Tutorial', postPublished = '2019-08-04';
```
I'm under the impression that a common use case is to repeat all values of the `INSERT` clause in the `UPDATE` clause again. This makes the code more verbose, more error-prone to write and less easy to machine-generate.

Having the option to not repeat the `INSERT` in the `UPDATE` would be preferable for me. Is that sensible? The syntax could be for example:
```sql
INSERT INTO BLOGPOSTs (postId, postTitle, postPublished)
VALUES (5, 'Python Tutorial', '2019-08-04')
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE;
```
There may be good reasons to allow the more complex syntax too, for cases where a specific update behavior is needed.

I can see a specific benefit in comparison to PostgreSQL's `ON CONFLICT` syntax which seems particularly verbose in my eyes. With PostgreSQL, its required to identify the conflicting keys in the statement. This seems significantly more error-prone, i.e. when tables change. Furthermore its very hard to machine-generate a PostgreSQL `UPSERT` statement that would work on an arbitrary table.

So what is the current workaround? If I'm loading data from multiple dfs to a table, how do the rest of you make sure that the repetitive rows from different dfs  are not left duplicated in the table or no error is raised? Thanks

@kuatroka this is a huge problem for us with basically all database systems. I'm not sure why there is no simpler alternative to the common `UPSERT` variants, that are all quite verbose and error-prone in my eyes.

I personally would love a statement that essentially does the same as inserting into an STL container like `std::set` or `std::map`: add if missing, otherwise overwrite.

Yes, but what do the devs in real apps use now as a workaround as it seems like a pretty big feature. 

Will checking if a record exists in the table before writing the pandas df help? I don't really see it because in this case the all the df records would need to be checked against the table one by one and it would defeat the purpose of the bulk insert. I feel I'm missing something or maybe I misunderstand the use case of Duckdb? Maybe it is not meant to be used a faster SQLite and instead it is just meant to be used (in-memory) as a help during data analysis workflow ?
Or to have a pipeline where first the data is loaded to SQLite with full SQL functionalities and later transferred to Duckdb for purely analytical work?

> I'll play with the idea of removing duplicates from the df prior to writing it to the DB.

That can work fine, but then you'll keep the values of the *earlier* occurrence, not the later. Is that what you want? For me, later inserts should overwrite earlier ones...

I deleted the post as I realised it didn't make much sense. Checking for the duplicates in the df prior to writing it to the DB, will not save me from checking for duplicates that might already be in the DB from the previous writes. In summary a proper `INSERT OR IGNORE` or `UPSERT` or `ON CONFLICT` SQL option is needed.

> Is there another open source database that implements this feature in a way that you particularly like? It always helps to have a good example! Thanks!

In case it helps, PG15 has implemented the `MERGE` statement:
* https://www.depesz.com/2022/03/31/waiting-for-postgresql-15-add-support-for-merge-sql-command/

review_comments: The `ON CONFLICT` does not seem to be fully supported for the `PhysicalBatchInsert` - perhaps remove this and instead always create a `PhysicalInsert` node when there is an `ON CONFLICT` clause - similar to what we do for the `RETURNING` clause?
